Adventure Toolbox
Those in small cities and large towns like Saringallow 
can afford some luxuries thanks to traveling merchants. 
Those in the countryside have no such luck and have 
become stubborn and resilient to survive. As those who 
have survived war and vowed to never face such loss 
again, these rural areas have fostered a strong sense of 
community. Neighbors tend to lend a hand without 
being asked and without expecting thanks, simply 
doing what needs to be done.
Spices are expensive for the countryside, making 
for bland meals. The typical Isgeri (outside Elidir) 
prefers an unsalted meal and will wrinkle their nose 
at heavily spiced cuisine. Porridges, roast chicken, 
and salads are common.
Fashion is usually the last thing on the mind of an 
Isgeri farmer, yet it’s still an important function of life. 
Hats are vital to keep the sun and wind from one’s 
eyes, and scarves protect from dust and cold. Those 
who are more fashion-forward dye their hats bright 
colors and decorate them with twigs and flowers, while 
knitters take pride in their families’ elaborate scarves. 
Symbols are often subtly woven into clothing, such as 
certain flowers for good luck or skulls to indicate hard 
times. Coloring one’s nails with a local flower’s dye 
has become popular, though such lacquers must be 
tough to withstand a full day’s labor.
Loyalty to Cheliax is mixed. Some fear and hate 
the patron nation, seeing it as the source of most of 
their troubles. Others can’t deny the good Cheliax did 
in the aftermath of the Goblinblood Wars and view 
the Church of Asmodeus positively, seeing both them 
and Cheliax as benevolent benefactors. Many young 
women were raised and indoctrinated by the Sisters of 
the Golden Erinys, who have a strong presence in the 
countryside. While some see such “charity” as a scam, 
no one can deny that Cheliax did help those in need.
Notable Figures
Alceo Demetrias (wise male aiuvarin human cleric of 
Milani 7) and Phoebe Demetrias (righteous female 
human commander 7) are the rebellious leaders of the 
Hellbreakers League, an organization formed to free 
Isger. More about them can be found on page 244.
Brakknap (haunted male goblin oracle 4) is a 
goblin elder working toward restoring humanoid 
and goblinoid relations. More information about 
Brakknap can be found on page 236.
The Isgeri Army is led by General Harwin Balefellow 
(principled male soldier 10), a stern man caught 
between his morals and his duty. Harwin is frustrated 
by the state of Isger but follows orders to a fault, 
secretly hoping for change yet unwilling to be the one 
to bring it about.
Hedvend VI has ruled Isger for decades, and his 
legacy won’t be a proud one. The ramifications of his 
decision to ignore the plight of the countryside during 
the Goblinblood Wars still echo throughout Isger to 
this day in the form of permanently wounded veterans, 
innumerable orphans, and towns completely wiped 
from the map. It’s well known that Hedvend cares 
only about pleasing Cheliax and is happy to let the rest 
of the nation fester so long as the elites are satisfied 
with their spoils.
The powerful daughter of Urgathoa, Illcayna 
Alonnor, has been working her machinations in 
the countryside for decades, infesting the land with 
undead. Her plans have largely run unhindered, 
thanks to the government’s lack of interest in the rural 
areas. More information about Illcayna can be found 
on page 242.
Lady Kaltessa Iyis (mysterious female human 
priestess of Mammon 20) is a seemingly immortal 
priestess of Mammon who has lived in the Menador 
Mountains for an uncounted period of time. 
Surrounded by devilish servants, she watches over the 
nation from her fortress while she plots on behalf of 
her master. These devils and her unnaturally long life 
are the result of an infernal pact with the archdevil 
Mammon as part of Kaltessa’s designs on ruling Isger, 
and perhaps one day, Cheliax as well. Her devotion to 
Mammon instead of Asmodeus makes her somewhat 
of a rogue element within the borders of Cheliax, so 
she plots and schemes from hundreds of miles away. 
With her acquisition of a warshard after the Godsrain 
and rising tensions between Cheliax and Andoran, 
Lady Iyis the Widow Queen is poised to make her 
move any day now.
For decades while the countryside was riddled with 
strife, Mama Grimclaw (devious female iron hag 9) 
had easy pickings among the numerous children left 
orphaned by the Goblinblood Wars. She keeps her 
victims hidden in a small town shielded from scrying 
magic. Illusions surround the town, ensuring that 
travelers pass by without a thought. In recent years, 
improvements in village sheriffs and security have 
made it more challenging for the hag to find victims, 
but Mama Grimclaw simply orders her current 
children to cause distractions so she can snatch up 
their newest sibling. Villages are coming to be aware 
of her brand of terror and warn their children to be 
good or the nightmare witch will get them—though 
Mama Grimclaw cares not for how good a child is, 
only that they’re easy to kidnap. Now, with the chaos 
of potential war sowing discord and fear throughout 
the nation, Mama Grimclaw has found plenty of new 
opportunities to prey on the vulnerable.

The most influential member among the Sisters of 
the Golden Erinys is Sister Marcella (pious human 
monk 6), an unassuming elderly woman who’s served 
the church of Asmodeus since she was a child. As the 
grand overseer of the sisterhood’s charities, she has 
great influence over the countryside thanks to the 
sisters’ stellar reputation. Marcella loves children and 
can often be found reading infernal passages from 
religious tomes to children too young to understand 
what they mean.
Varskand Gilwrad (vengeful male human bigot 8)
is a veteran of the Goblinblood Wars and one of the 
founders of the notorious Isgeri Slayers. He lost his 
home and his left eye to hobgoblin raiders and has 
never forgiven goblinkind for its sins against him. 
Varskand sees himself and his gang as crusaders, doing 
the work no one else will by taking up the sword to 
enact justice that the government has failed to serve. He 
works hard to pass off the Isgeri Slayers as a legitimate 
organization of mercenaries and adventurers rather 
than what they truly are: angry bigots.
Notable Locations
With small villages and farmsteads dotting the 
landscape, Isger is full of locations to visit or explore. 
Below are a few of the country’s most interesting or 
important locations.
Breachill: This small town is relatively young 
compared to other Isgeri settlements. Situated in 
the shadow of the Five Kings Mountains, its origins 
are similarly shrouded in mystery, as the first people 
found there in 4520 ar were 50 humans with no 
memory of who they were or how they got there. A 
passing wizard named Lamond Breachton discovered 
this outpost and helped its lost inhabitants build 
up their camp into a full-fledged town. Though he 
couldn’t uncover their past, the grateful villagers 
named the town after him. As Breachill’s population 
grew over the years, Lamond Breachton remained 
to guide them in a paternal fashion until he one 
day disappeared. The townsfolk erected a statue in 
his honor and continued his legacy of benevolence. 
Breachill’s peaceful populace attracted the attention 
of the newly formed Hellknight Order of the Nail, 
who built their citadel 10 miles northeast of the town 
in 4638. Though they were lured to Korvosa by Queen 
Domina only 44 years later, the citadel still stands. 
In recent months, rumors spread that Breachill 
was harboring members of the Hellbreakers League, 
and Hellknights from the Order of the Rack quickly

Chitterwood: This old-growth forest is home to 
many tribes of goblins, though markedly fewer since 
the end of the Goblinblood Wars. Far more dangerous 
creatures lurk among the trees. Detailed information 
about the Chitterwood can be found in the article 
starting on page 180.
Citadel Altaerein: Only a short distance from 
Breachill, this Hellknight citadel was built as the 
base of operations for the Order of the Nail before 
they moved to Korvosa in 4682. The building housed 
fewer than three dozen Hellknights for the following 
decades until it was completely abandoned in 4711. 
Goblins moved into the lower and basement levels of 
the citadel in 4717, but they were targeted by a cult 
of Norgorber who was defeated by a group of heroes 
only two years later. After defeating a manifestation 
of Dahak, the heroes gifted the citadel to the town of 
Breachill. However, the Godsrain brought more strife 
to the area, and when Hellknights from the Order of 
the Rack marched into Breachill, they also occupied 
Citadel Altaerein. Recently, a major battle between 
those Hellknights and Andoran’s Eagle Knights 
occurred in the surrounding area, part of which 
included a siege of the citadel. Once again, ownership 
of the fortress changed hands after the Hellknights 
were routed in the Battle of Hellknight Hill, and its 
future providence is now uncertain.
Citadel Dinyar: Located among the peaks of the 
Aspodell Mountains, this sturdy fortress serves as the 
headquarters for the Hellknight Order of the Godclaw. 
After the recent change in the deities promoted 
by this religious order and the looming threat 
of war between Cheliax and Andoran, many 
Hellknights at Citadel Dinyar have begun venturing 
forth into the countryside with more regularity. 
Rather than demand obedience like so many other 
Hellknight orders, those who worship the pantheon 
known as the Talons of the Godclaw have been focused 
more on educating the common folk on the everyday 
benefits of an ordered and disciplined life. Friction 
with the more traditional Hellknights of the Godclaw 
has forced many of these worshippers to return to the 
citadel to ensure newly enlisted armigers aren’t overly 
influenced against their newer philosophy.
Dustpawn: The citizens of this once prosperous 
iron mining town near the Drumish border built a 
thriving industry around the town’s many goats after 
the mines were exhausted. Merchants from all over 
Isger, Druma, and Andoran regularly visit to purchase 
the town’s goat milk, butter, cheese, meat, and hides. 
This constant trade traffic also makes the caravans 
traveling the roads into and out of Dustpawn prime 
targets for bandits, many of whom make their 
hideouts in the former mining tunnels. Recently, 
Elladas Demos, a smuggler who extorted money from 
the Dustpawn government to keep bandit attacks to a 
minimum, was found decapitated in the town square. 
Some say she was targeted by House Thrune after 
spreading conspiracy theories about Abrogail II’s 
lineage. Others believe she faked her death to live a 
life of luxury in Druma after hoarding several years’ 
worth of monetary gains. Since her death, though, 
merchants have become wary of making the journey 
to Dustpawn for fear of the bandits. The town’s 
current mayor, Ruprecht Haesmith (anxious male 
human politician 1), has repeatedly sent requests for 
aid from Elidir to no avail.
Elidir: Situated at the junction where the Summerun 
River merges with the North Conerica River, Isger’s

capital is a hub of trade from Molthune, Druma, and 
even from the more distant Cheliax. The city escaped 
much of the damage caused by the Goblinblood Wars, 
being over 100 miles away from the Chitterwood. 
This remoteness allowed the Isgeri government to 
continue to function normally during the conflict, 
but many soldiers and villagers now feel this safety 
was undeserved, especially since the officials and 
generals in Elidir couldn’t put an end to the war 
without help from neighboring nations. Some even

of the nation’s common folk. As such, the average 
Isgeri farmer tends to sneer when talking about Elidir, 
believing its residents to be no better than fools. 
Somewhat ironically, the Chelaxian government has 
similar views of Hedvend VI, Isger’s current steward. 
Though he’s served Cheliax faithfully for decades, 
many Chelaxian nobles believe the country should be 
in more capable hands. Rumors of his replacement 
have been swirling around Elidir for over five years, 
but for whatever reason, Cheliax has yet to send the 
order. Hedvend is painfully aware of this looming 
threat, and his closest allies have been encouraging 
him to act with more boldness, especially in light of the 
recent defeat of the Hellknights at Citadel Altaerein.

Chitterwood, 
Fernsby 
has 
a

strained 
relationship with the nearby artist colony of Stumpfield. 
More information can be found on page 40.
Finder’s Gulch: Illcayna Alonnor is the undisputed 
master of this haunted place. Once a simple and remote 
quarry town, Finder’s Gulch was overrun by malicious 
undead several decades ago. Illcayna, priestess of 
Urgathoa, followed the horde of wights to establish 
a base of operations from which she has continually 
raided other Isgeri villages, Cheliax, and Molthune, all 
to grow the ranks of her undead armies. Over time, 
Illcayna wishes to turn Isger’s entire populace to the 
worship of her god, though this goal will likely need 
to be achieved by force. More about Finder’s Gulch 
and Illcayna Alonnor can be found on pages 125 and 
242, respectively.
Gillamoor: Located at the edge of the Chitterwood, 
Gillamoor survived both attacks from goblins and 
several fires that claimed much of the nearby forest, 
only to fall to a curse of undeath. As part of her 
campaign to infest all of Isger with undead, Illcayna 
Alonnor chose Gillamoor because of its tragic history 
and, consequently, its rather large graveyard. Hoping 
the town would soon be overrun with undead, she laid 
a curse on the settlement, making it so that anyone 
who perished within Gillamoor would quickly rise as 
a brain-eating zombie. To light the fuse of this mystical 
bomb, Illcayna then used her necromantic powers to 
raise a few zombies from the Gillamoor cemetery in the 
dead of night. The first death occurred hours later, and 
though the original zombies were destroyed, the chain 
reaction had already begun. Within weeks, the entire 
population of Gillamoor had perished or fled. The Isgeri 
military quarantined the area, believing the tragedy to 
have been caused by plague, but they soon abandoned 
their post when no plague could be detected.
Good Home: This small town was abandoned 
during the Goblinblood Wars and taken over by Mama 
Grimclaw, who renamed it Good Home. She raises 
her numerous kidnapped children here, shielding the 
town with magic so no one will notice it. The town 
is in working condition, with the kidnapped children 
learning to be self-sufficient so that they never have to 
leave. Travelers who wander too close are sometimes 
murdered so Mama Grimclaw can gift her children 
with their possessions.
Haugin’s Ear: The inhabitants of this quiet fishing 
village trade their daily catches, as well as cured 
fish, with passing vessels on the River Keld—mostly 
Chelaxian military and trade ships—and to miners 
panning for gold in the Aspodell foothills. A few 
families also make a living selling tamed firefoot 
fennecs, which are regarded as symbols of good luck 
by many in the region. Haugin’s Ear is named after 
an unusual 30-foot-tall outcropping of rock along the 
riverbank near its docks that resembles the half-buried 
head and ear of a giant lying on his side. Legends claim 
this stony protrusion is part of the petrified remains of 
Haugin, a flesh-eating giant who ran afoul of a Taldan 
wizard centuries ago. Occasionally, treasure hunters 
from outside Isger venture to the area in search of 
shattered pieces of Haugin, which are rumored to hold 
great power. In years past, many believed the stone head 
was somehow luring children inside, but in truth, these 
missing children were devoured by a sweet hag named 
Marjulla, who was recently discovered and slain by one 
of the visiting treasure hunters. With her dying words, 
Marjulla warned of retribution from her two sisters.
Iron Rose: With its elaborate stone arches, this 
palace flaunts its Chelaxian influence for all who 
dare to approach. Centuries ago, Lady Kaltessa Iyis 
staked her claim on a lush valley near the border of 
Druma and conscripted dozens of devils to build the 
impressive edifice she calls home. The opulent fortress 
is rumored to be filled with enough gold to buy entire 
nations, though no one has ever had the privilege to 
step inside and find out.

Merrywim: This small riverside town was mainly 
known for its shell jewelry; beyond that, its people eked 
out a quiet living in the countryside. That all changed 
after the Godsrain. Now, the people of Merrywim 
have become rambunctious, throwing enormous 
parties nightly and often drinking until sundown. The 
realization that even a god can fall terrified the town’s 
inhabitants so much that they’ve become hedonistic 
nihilists, intent on enjoying their lives as much as they 
possibly can. However, of late the partying has had 
to stop because of a mysterious creature that’s been 
spotted in the Conerica River, something massive 
enough to be a threat to those who live ashore. A few 
brave fishers banded together to capture the beast but 
returned with only broken nets and lines. It seems that 
professional adventurers might be the solution for this 
issue, which the town is eager to address so that they 
can return to their frantic revelry.
Logas: Once the capital of Isger, the scars of the 
Goblinblood Wars, both physical and mental, can 
still be found in this riverside city’s architecture and 
citizens. Logas was continually under siege during the 
conflict, leading to a lasting distrust of goblinoids. The 
city’s current mayor, Valenia Remingward (progressive 
female human politician 2), fought in the war but 
ceased the practice of regularly firing trebuchets into 
the nearby Chitterwood and dismantled the display of 
goblin skulls along the city walls immediately after her 
appointment in 4723. These mandates caused some 
consternation among the city’s nobles, who claimed 
that Mayor Remingward’s policies would be seen as 
a sign of weakness by the goblin tribes and ignite a 
second round of hostilities. Most of their complaints 
have been silenced in the wake of recent events as 
Hellknights amass within the city, either fleeing from 
their defeat at the Battle of Hellknight Hill or arriving 
from across the Chelaxian border as reinforcements. 
Tensions run high in Logas, though the majority of its 
citizens support Chelaxian rule over Isger.
Saringallow: Centuries ago, this city began as a 
small garden estate named Sarini’s Hollow, founded 
by House Sarini of Cheliax, a minor noble house. Over 
time, it slowly grew into a village with its own farms, 
shops, and trade via the nearby river. Though it seemed 
idyllic from the outside, it harbored a sinister secret. 
The nobles of House Sarini dabbled in diabolism long 
before House Thrune rose to power, and their hideous 
rituals resulted in the deaths of several of the village’s 
young people. The citizens rebelled and hung every 
member of House Sarini they could find. The town 
was then nicknamed Sarini Gallows, which over time 
evolved into the city’s current name. The Sarini estate 
still stands as a grim warning to other Chelaxian 
nobles who might think to take advantage of the 
populace, and they ensure that noble outsiders don’t 
feel welcome, especially if their last name is Sarini. 
The city’s history is likely the reason that Hellbreakers 
League activity is most prevalent there, leading 
many to believe that Saringallow is the rebellious 
organization’s headquarters. More about Saringallow 
can be found in the article starting on page 200.
Stumpfield: Founded by goblin and human artists, 
Stumpfield is a haven for creators of all stripes. It 
relies on trading with nearby Fernsby for much of its 
practical goods. More information can be found on 
pages 30 and 39.
Swiftrun: This small village is most known for its 
priests of Erastil who teach how to homestead and 
defend one’s community. The community is nearly all 
Erastilian, with an emphasis on helping one another. 
Rather than individual gardening, the village has an 
enormous community garden that everyone takes 
turns caring for. Everything is shared in the village, 
from tools to carts, and hospitality is seen as the 
greatest virtue.
Twin Horns: This nunnery of the Sisters of the 
Golden Erinys lies in the Aspodell Mountains, quietly 
serving as a place for aspiring young women to train as 
sisters. The convent is small and its training rigorous, 
the nuns practicing both religious duties and martial 
arts from dawn to dusk. Many of the girls raised in the 
sisters’ orphanages end up traveling here to become 
nuns. Recently, the nunnery discovered a piece of a 
warshard that affected their livestock, turning their 
goats into dawnsilver.
Umok: This centuries-old gnome village has 
outlawed fire within 500 yards of its buildings due 
to past run-ins with fire-loving goblins from the 
Chitterwood. The residents now use alchemy and 
magic for heat and light. More information about 
Umok can be found on pages 30 and 36.
Vordia: After the Goblinblood Wars, the Sisters of 
the Golden Erinys and, by extension, the Church of 
Asmodeus worked hard to rebuild Vordia and take 
care of its citizens. As such, its citizens are generally 
grateful and loyal to Cheliax. Vordia is the proud 
location of one of the first orphanages built by the 
sisters after the wars. More information can be found 
on pages 30 and 32.
Wolfpoint: A reserve garrison for the Isgeri army, 
Wolfpoint has been left empty since the Battle of 
Hellknight Hill, its soldiers called to active duty in 
other parts of the country. As a result, the local river 
bandits have grown bolder and often use Wolfpoint as 
a meeting place. More information about Wolfpoint 
can be found on page 30.

Welcome to the Chitterwood
Isger is a land of many scars, both literal and 
metaphorical, and no place better illustrates this 
quality than the once-dense hardwood forest known 
as the Chitterwood. Located in southern Isger near 
the Conerica River, the Aspodell Mountains, and the 
city of Logas, the Chitterwood has long been home 
to hundreds of goblinoid tribes. It’s also home to a 
trade route favored by smugglers. Travel through these 
woods has always been a risky affair due to the threat 
of bandits, but desperate and unsavory travelers are 
willing to traverse the Chitterwood to stay off Isger’s 
main roads.
Due to the area’s unsavory reputation, most 
preferred to avoid the Chitterwood as much as 
possible and maintained little contact with its 
goblinoid residents. This situation suddenly changed 
in 4697 ar, when hobgoblin commanders and their 
goblin armies launched a series of deadly attacks 
against Isger’s rural settlements. The Goblinblood 
Wars, as the conflicts became known, lasted for 
four intensely bloody years. Scores of goblin and 
hobgoblin forces spread across the region, leaving 
death and devastation in their wake. From Varisia to 
Taldor, entire towns were destroyed in the carnage. 
Forces from Andoran, Cheliax, and Druma allied to 
fight the threat. When the Goblinblood Wars at last 
came to an end, the victorious alliance of Drumish 
mercenaries, Eagle Knights, and Hellknights burned 
most of the Chitterwood to the ground.
Despite the massive ecological damage it sustained, 
the Chitterwood isn’t entirely devoid of fauna. Birds 
still sing, bears and boars still roam, and silk moths 
can sometimes be found munching on mulberry 
leaves. Stories of a fierce and ancient beast persist, 
said to now be a living shadow, and the beast is 
rumored to still be on the hunt.
The Caverns of the Chitterwood
The Goblinblood Wars claimed a staggering number of 
lives on all sides, but for the goblin tribes, subjugated 
by hobgoblin commanders and hunted by the 
genocidal Isgeri Slayers, the conflict brought almost 
total annihilation. With most of the Chitterwood a 
smoldering ruin, there remained only one place for 
the surviving goblins to flee: underground.
Deep beneath the remains of the Chitterwood lies a 
vast network of caverns and warrens—an ideal, if less 
than pleasant, place for a devastated people to hide, 
regroup, and rebuild. Much to the tribes’ annoyance, 
however, the caverns were already home to a number 
of creatures who weren’t exactly keen to share their 
space. The bats and rats at least proved tolerably tasty, 
but the cave bears were another story altogether; the 
People of the Swarm tribe, which already had over 
190 songs graphically describing the danger of bear 
attacks, soon added new songs specifically warning 
about cave bears.
Surviving the caverns of Chitterwood for an 
extended period is difficult for several reasons 
outside of ursine encounters. The only light to be 
found is near the cave entrances, humidity is high, 
and food is limited. Fortunately for goblins, their 
darkvision, resourcefulness, and ability to digest 
pretty much anything organic means they’re better 
suited for living in caves than most other Golarion 
residents. Goblins prefer meat when they can get 
it—rats make a good stew, and bats pickle well—but 
most of their diet in the caverns consists of fungi and 
insects, with frogs and fish occasionally rounding 
out the menu.
Every once in a while, sometimes out of boredom 
and sometimes on a dare, a cavern-dwelling goblin 
risks a trip to the world above in search of tastier 
eats or shiny new treasures. This is generally frowned 
upon by the eldest tribe members, whose parents 
and grandparents were survivors of the war; visibly 
scarred and deeply afraid, that first generation passed 
their understandable fear on to their children. Younger 
goblins who have never known life outside the caverns 
are more willing to explore the world above, even 
when not patrolling or hunting. Some particularly 
wise goblin leaders have begun the delicate process of 
reestablishing diplomatic relations with non-goblins 
to better deal with the increasing threat of undead 
roaming the countryside.
Inhabitants
Aboveground and below, the Chitterwood’s population 
is higher than many realize. While goblins represent the 
largest percentage of residents, one can also find a small 
number of hobgoblins and even non-goblinoids here.
Chitterwood

===== Page 183 =====
182
CHITTERWOOD GOBLINS
Six generations have passed for goblinoids since the 
end of the Goblinblood Wars. During that time, many, 
if not most, goblins in Isger have called the caverns of 
Chitterwood home. While tribes like the 
People of the Swarm, Spine 
Threshers, and True Hoard 
are well known, hundreds of 
goblinoid cultures live in or 
beneath the Chitterwood, only a 
few of which are presented here. 
Some traits common across goblin 
society—fear of dogs and horses, love 
of song and fire, and wariness of the 
written word—endure among the 
goblins of the Chitterwood despite 
their horrific losses and subsequent 
displacement. Significant differences 
exist, however; in the war’s aftermath, 
distinctions between cultural groups deepened as 
each dealt with the experience in their own way. The 
People of the Swarm tribe, for example, sings inspiring 
fight songs about taking revenge on their former 
hobgoblin commanders, while the Spine Threshers 
tribe excels in combat. The Hookback tribe, which 
now resides in the caves of the southern Chitterwood, 
takes its name from the particularly vicious torture it 
endured during the war. Surviving Hookback goblins 
inflicted their children with the same permanent, 
bone-deep piercings that had been forced upon them, 
transforming their pain into a symbol of survival and 
rite of passage into adulthood.
Before the Goblinblood Wars, goblins of the 
Chitterwood, like many forest goblins, tended to 
be fairly reclusive. This inclination doesn’t mean 
they weren’t dangerous when they wanted to be, 
however. Contact with non-goblinoids was generally 
limited, with the notable exception of scavenging and 
stealing from unwary travelers who passed through 
their territory. Goblin ambushes, when they did 
happen, could be as fierce as they were chaotic—a 
fact that hobgoblin commanders exploited for their 
own ends. The terror of the war reinforced the 
Chitterwood goblins’ desire to keep to themselves as 
much as possible. With virtually all of their warriors 
dead, those goblins who survived the war were left 
largely defenseless. Today, goblins typically venture 
aboveground only when necessary and preferably 
under cover of night, lest they be discovered by 
someone bigger and more dangerous.
Some smaller tribes chose not to flee to the caverns 
at all, for different reasons and with mixed results. 
The area along the burned edges of the Chitterwood 
is home to the Bulbhead tribe, whose name comes 
from their distinctive practice of wearing masks made 
from gourds. During the war, sadistic hobgoblins 
commanders forced their goblin troops to wear 
gourds filled with wasps or spiders; goblins 
reclaimed their power by wearing 
masks on their own and robbing the 
hobgoblins of their fun. The crude 
masks are of dubious help in battle, 
but Bulbhead warriors make 
formidable foes nonetheless.
 The Cinder Seekers are not 
actually a tribe at all, but rather 
an activist movement. Members 
travel throughout the Chitterwood on 
a mission to ensure that goblins never 
serve hobgoblins again. With arson as 
their weapon of choice, they take fiery 
vengeance against hobgoblins and their 
goblin collaborators.
Floods are common along the eastern edge of the 
Chitterwood, yet this area is where the tiny Mudrub 
tribe claims territory. As their name suggests, these 
goblins prefer to coat themselves in a thick layer 
of swamp muck and abhor any attempt to wash it 
off. During the war, hobgoblins punished Mudrub 
goblins by branding them with words. Survivors, 
ashamed and desperate to remove them, turned to 
burning and scarring themselves where they’d been 
branded, and eventually they began marking their 
children in a new tradition. Rejecting the written 
word, Mudrub goblins burn and scar their children 
with random patterns or images.
In some cases, the decision to not take refuge 
in the caverns has paid off. The Crookedtoes tribe 
became travelers and adventurers, journeying as far as 
Absalom and becoming valued allies to the Knights 
of Lastwall. The Dragondweller tribe has likewise 
provided aid to various human nations, earning the 
respect and protection of their allies.
BULBHEAD
Bulbhead goblins are distinguished by their iconic 
gourd helmets, a cultural fashion statement that ties 
back to the Goblinblood Wars. While the helmets were 
once used as tools of torment against these goblins, 
they now wear them with pride, having overcome the 
humiliation and pain their hobgoblin leaders inflicted 
upon them. Even babies wear tiny gourds, which are 
said to help shape their heads to be nice and round. 
This penchant for gourds also makes these goblins 
famous for pumpkin recipes such as mashed gourd 
and rat stew and caramelized pumpkin squares.
Bulbhead goblin

The Bulbhead goblins are loosely nomadic, living 
in tents as they move about the border of the woods. 
These tents are covered in leaves and sticks to blend in 
with the brush, granting the goblins both shelter and 
camouflage. While they might settle in one spot for a 
week or so, they never stay too long to avoid enemies 
pinning down their locations. The Bulbhead goblins 
always make sure to mark the best spots with patches 
of gourds so they can return at harvest.
Life on the edges of the Chitterwood has the Bulbhead 
goblins interacting with non-goblinoids more than 
any other goblin tribe. While the early days postwar 
had high tensions between goblins and humanoids, 
the Bulbheads have learned that humanoids can be 
either friend or foe and adapted accordingly. Bulbhead 
goblins are now known for setting up small pop-up 
stalls to trade goods from within the Chitterwood with 
merchants and abandoning said stalls the moment they 
sense danger. They’re some of the most social goblins 
around, easily haggling with traders and happily selling 
flora and fauna from deeper within the woods.
These interactions with non-goblinoids have also 
pitted the Bulbheads against the Isgeri Slayers, a 
bigoted anti-goblin organization. The Bulbheads 
loathe the Slayers and take every opportunity they 
can to humiliate them, raiding their camps and leaving 
gourds as taunts so the Slayers know exactly who 
sabotaged them. They’ll even set tents aflame with 
Slayers sleeping inside without remorse, declaring that 
war is war and so is this!
Bulbhead goblins make fierce enemies and even 
fiercer friends, happy to share their bounty with any 
who come to them with open arms. They don’t trend 
toward adventuring, but the occasional Bulbhead has 
gone off to become a daring fighter and returned with 
even better helms than gourds.
CINDER SEEKERS
The Cinder Seekers are a group of goblins determined 
to remember history and learn from its mistakes. This 
movement is small but fervent, spreading among the 
older generations of goblins. They constantly recall 
the atrocities of the Goblinblood Wars and the cruelty 
from hobgoblins against their people, and they’ve 
vowed to ensure such oppression never happens again.
History is preserved in powerful dirges about the 
wickedness of hobgoblins and the plight of goblins, 
though some would argue that these songs are highly 
biased and even bigoted. Hobgoblins are depicted 
as monstrous oppressors and all goblins as innocent 
victims, ignoring the fact that some goblin tribes were 
quite willing to join in the war against their humanoid 
neighbors. Many Cinder Seekers tend to look at all 
hobgoblins with suspicion and paranoia, sure that 
they have an agenda. The most zealous Cinder Seekers 
attack hobgoblins indiscriminately, while those wiser 
will take the time to discern one’s intentions.
The Cinder Seekers believe that the purifying force 
of fire will burn away both their enemies and the 
will to harm them, making their pyromania almost 
fanatical. The Cinder Seekers persist in hunting down 
any who might try and repeat history and burn them 
with fire to ensure the past stays in the past. If peace 
comes to the Chitterwood, it’ll likely be in spite of the 
Cinder Seekers rather than because of them.
HOOKBACK
The deep caverns beneath the Chitterwood are home 
to the Hookback tribe, where goblins distinguish 
themselves with unique piercings. The Hookback 
goblins have learned to see even in the darkest cave 
and listen for the smallest footsteps, aiding them in 
the endless shadows of the underground. Because of 
this, most Hookback goblins are reluctant to breach 
the surface with its painfully bright light, preferring to 
dwell in the shadows.
The Hookback tribe’s most meaningful practice 
stems from a tragic history of torment and pain. 
Survivors of grievous torture during the Goblinblood 
Wars were ashamed of their piercings, signs of 
weakness that they were, until a brave young goblin 
declared that they wished to be pierced as well to 
honor the pain of their people. With that, a tradition 
was born, and now all Hookback goblins take the 
piercings when they come of age.
Having lived in the deep caverns of the Chitterwood 
for several generations, Hookback goblins are expert 
foragers, scouring the dark for what little nutrition 
there is to find. They farm mushrooms and lichen as 
well as fish and newts.
The tribe sees creatures of the dark as their brethren 
and fears the light, making them the unusual goblin 
tribe that isn’t pyromaniacal. Fire is reserved for the 
creation of piercings and for special ceremonies, where 
the tribe gathers for a coming of age or to tell stories 
of the past; it’s feared and revered, the greatest light of 
all, and the one that destroyed their original homes in 
the Chitterwood. For the Hookback goblins, darkness 
is preferred to a light that burns.
MUDRUB
The small Mudrub tribe is rarely seen without a thick 
layer of muck and mud across their bodies, covering up 
the burn scars that mark them as Mudrub. They were 
once branded with words and took to fire to remove 
the evil of literacy from their bodies, turning it into

===== Page 185 =====
184
tradition to burn artful patterns into their members—
though it’s rare for strangers to see said patterns, as a 
Mudrub goblin is sure to be covered in filth. It’s a great 
sign of intimacy and respect for a Mudrub goblin to 
remove the muck on their skin and reveal their burns 
to someone.
Being a small tribe, Mudrub goblins prefer hiding to 
fighting, using their superior stealth skills to slink into 
the muddy banks and lie still until danger has passed. 
The thick coating of muck hides their scent, and they 
have no issue with waiting for hours in a comfortable 
spot. Few Mudrub goblins adventure outside of their 
home domain, uncomfortable anywhere their muddy 
second skin can’t conceal them.
The tribe lives in tall mud huts structured to last 
through flooding season, with paths of rocks that 
can be used as stepping stones when the waters rise. 
Though they take precautions to keep themselves 
out of dangerously high waters, Mudrub goblins are 
expert swimmers. They’re often compared to frogs as 
they sweep through brush and muck, darting around 
their swampy environment with ease. This comparison 
has led to them calling their children tadpoles, with 
coming of age jokingly described as “becoming a 
frog.” They use bird calls to communicate from afar 
and stay hidden, content to observe rather than 
interact with strangers.
Living in the flooded eastern Chitterwood, the 
Mudrub goblin diet relies on frogs. They camouflage 
in the mud and detritus to sneak up on and then 
snatch their unsuspecting prey with their bare hands. 
They enjoy their meals both raw and cooked, and 
they also catch snakes and birds as part of their diet. 
Pickled frog legs are a popular snack as are fried 
snake heads.
PEOPLE OF THE SWARM
Goblins sneak and goblins spring
Goblins swarm and goblins sting
Trap the hob and slice their gut
Goblins here to blow them up!
Break the chains and beat the drum
Burn their bread and steal the rum,
All the blood we goblins shed
Now goblins rise and they be dead!
—People of the Swarm anti-hobgoblin song of resistance
One of the largest and most prominent of Isger’s 
goblin tribes, the People of the Swarm have long 
been famous—or infamous, depending on one’s 
perspective—for the tactics they employ when on the 
offensive. Though goblins aren’t generally known for 
their ability or willingness to effectively organize, it’s 
a hallmark of the People of the Swarm tribe. Early 
on in their history, they realized that working as a 
group meant that more of them were likely to survive 
a fight and come away with whatever treasures they 
were seeking. Where a single goblin might be unable 
to take down a target, a group of goblins can. Swarm 
goblins work together in battle to distract and 
overwhelm their target as they “sting” with arrows, 
daggers, and dogslicers. Members of this tribe tend to 
make successful rogues, even if subtlety is sometimes 
a challenge.
Still, there are limits to the tribe’s favored 
approach—a fact they learned the hard way when 
some particularly hungry Swarm goblins tried to 
turn a grizzly bear into a meal for the tribe. Lest this 
lesson be forgotten, the People of the Swarm have 
nearly 200 songs describing in gory detail the horror 
of bear attacks. Their repertoire of bear songs grew 
when they fled to the Caverns of Chitterwood and 
discovered the cave bears living there.
If there’s one thing that goblins are known for 
(other than how much they love fire), it’s their ability 
to adapt. The first Swarm goblins to take refuge in 
the caverns had little interest in fighting; they were 
scared and traumatized, and most, if not all, of their 
warriors were dead. They wandered the caves,

stumbled across a massive colony of bats. Disturbing 
thousands of bats results in more noise and chaos 
than most folks can handle, but to the People of the 
Swarm, it was a sign they’d found their spot. In this 
safe place, the tribe began to heal and regrow their 
numbers. The elders sang about the wars, their old 
lives, and the mighty heroes lost, and as the tribe 
sang, they strengthened. Now they sing songs not 
only about bear attacks and legendary deeds, but also 
resilience. One day, goblins will be many again, and 
hobgoblins few. There’s power in the swarm.
To this tribe, bats are kindred spirits; they only 
sleep where it’s safe to do so, they forage at night, 
and they almost always leave their caves as a group. 
While goblins can’t hang upside down from the cave 
ceiling, the Swarm did learn the importance of not 
sleeping on the ground—better, instead, to be as high 
as possible, away from floodwaters and out of the 
easy reach of cave bears. Adult members of the tribe 
seek out goblin-sized nooks and crannies to sleep 
in, atop simple bedding made from animal hides or 
plants gathered during nighttime excursions above. 
Children are kept in enclosures nestled into nooks of 
their own near the adults.
Swarm goblins are also expert rock climbers, 
learning to climb as soon as they can walk. They’ve 
adapted the traditional swarming techniques to 
make greater use of height and even sound. Taking 
inspiration from bats, the tribe learned how to 
navigate the caves by paying attention to what 
they heard. Darkvision only works so far, after all, 
and fire doesn’t always stay lit in the dampness of 
the caves. Swarm goblins have developed a way to 
communicate with each other in a series of clicks, 
chirps, and other sounds that make up a language 
only they understand.
SPINE THRESHERS
Of all the goblin tribes in the Chitterwood, the Spine 
Threshers might be the one best known for skill in 
combat. Whereas the People of the Swarm prefer 
to attack on foot, the Spine Threshers rely heavily 
on mounted combat, excelling in the art as an act 
of devotion to their favored creator god, Zarongel. 
During the Goblinblood Wars, hobgoblin commanders 
used members of this tribe to carry out particularly 
vicious attacks, caring little about whether they or 
their mounts—typically goblin dogs or wolves—
survived for long. By the end of the wars, there were 
precious few Spine Thresher warriors alive. Those who 
made it to safety were determined that their knowledge 
wouldn’t be lost.
When they first arrived in the caverns, the Spine 
Thresher tribe had little apart from some of their 
mounts, which were simply too important to 
leave behind; the tribe’s physical survival, and 
the survival of their culture, depended upon these 
creatures. The Spine Threshers trace their founding 
to a warrior whose mount was a gift from Zarongel 
himself, a reward for her great skill and devotion. 
Regrowing the tribe meant increasing not only the 
goblin population, but that of their animals as well. 
Today, the Spine Threshers claim one of the larger 
territories in the caverns. A sizable portion of their 
area is dedicated to the care and training of their 
mounts and the warriors who ride them. A favorite 
pastime involves mounted Spine Threshers racing 
through an extensive, often cramped, network of 
naturally formed tunnels. It’s an exhilarating and 
dangerous game that serves as an important proving 
ground for young warriors.
The Spine Threshers are also particularly fond 
of dares. If there’s a goblin sneaking topside to 
do something foolhardy (or brave, as they see it), 
it’s frequently someone from this tribe. Hunting 
is fun, but it isn’t enough; young warriors who 
grew up hearing songs about the before times are 
eager to have a chance to fight and make names 
for themselves like the heroes of past generations 
did. Games and dares help channel some of their 
growing restlessness and keep their skills honed.
Unsurprisingly, members of this tribe make 
effective fighters and rangers, but some serve 
their people in other ways. Those who feel an 
especially strong connection to fire might become 
a pyrokineticist; despite goblins’ usual misgivings 
about magic, those who command fire are thought 
to be favored by Zarongel. Given the tribe’s deep 
understanding of animals and their zeal for hunting, 
some members of the tribe become effective rangers. 
In stark contrast to the People of the Swarm, the 
Spine Threshers regard cave bears with awe, 
considering them role models in combat, but wisely 
never attempt to train them as either companions 
or mounts. Whatever role they occupy in the tribe, 
Spine Threshers goblins, like cave bears, tend to be 
aggressively territorial and rarely end a fight until 
they know their foe is dead.
TRUE HOARD
Those encountering the True Hoard goblin tribe for 
the first time typically underestimate these goblins’ 
talents and capabilities. Unlike the Spine Threshers, 
True Hoard goblins don’t make fighting their priority, 
preferring to scavenge, steal, or create. They’re

===== Page 187 =====
186
gatherers more than hunters, though they can and do 
hunt quite well when the need arises; when it comes 
to fashioning snares, nets, or clever traps, few are as 
talented as the goblins of the True Hoard. During 
the Goblinblood Wars, the tribe very nearly lost 
their knowledge of such things since most of their 
skilled trap makers and hunters were conscripted 
by hobgoblins and subsequently perished in battle. 
What the survivors did know, they passed on to their 
children, and everything else the tribe rediscovered 
along the way through trial and error.
Endlessly curious and innovative, True Hoard 
goblins make the most of everything they have. It’s a 
trait that’s served them well in the caverns; knowing 
how to make something out of junk and something 
tasty (or at least edible) out of scraps and detritus 
means the difference between life and death. True 
Hoard goblins rarely throw anything away, even 
items that seem totally useless to everyone else. 
Maybe not today, and maybe not tomorrow, but 
someday—they’re sure of it!—whatever it is will be 
just the thing they need. And of course, if it’s shiny or 
pretty, it doesn’t need a purpose. It’s a treasure! 
This belief actually puts them in an odd relationship 
with a particular species of rat living in the caverns: 
the bushy-tailed woodrat. Most folks in Isger who 
have encountered woodrats call them pack rats; the 
True Hoard calls them gully-rakers. Like the True 
Hoard tribe, woodrats love shiny things and spend a 
great deal of their time and energy collecting treasures 
and stashing them in their nests. Some treasures 
are edible, but most aren’t—they’re just pretty or 
interesting in some way. Woodrats will even drop 
what they’re carrying if they come across something 
they find more interesting. 
When it rains in the Chitterwood, floodwaters rush 
into the caverns, bringing all manner of debris, muck, 
and sometimes delightful surprises; True Hoard 
goblins and woodrats frequently clash over who 
gets to claim which items. Despite their irritation, 
the True Hoard has a degree of respect for woodrats 
and even finds them useful (and occasionally 
tasty). Finding a woodrat’s nest sometimes yields 
amazing finds, provided the items haven’t been 
“claimed” yet; woodrats urinate on their stash, and 
eventually everything gets stuck in place so firmly 
that nothing can be removed. Figuring out what 
to do with woodrat urine–soaked items actually 
led some members to make fascinating discoveries. 
As they eventually realized, there are lots of useful 
components in woodrat waste!
After six generations of exploration, discovery, and 
experimentation, the tribe is better equipped than 
ever for a fight should one come their way. Today, 
if you meet a goblin alchemist or inventor in Isger, 
there’s a good chance they’re from the True Hoard 
tribe. Their formulas aren’t recorded in words, so 
anyone attempting to understand a goblin alchemist’s 
notes will have a hard time of it, and the True Hoard 
prefers it that way.
HOBGOBLINS
With the establishment of Oprak in 4717 ar, 
hobgoblins now have a nation to call home. Though 
seemingly small in size, Oprak is rich in resources both 
natural and wondrous and is thriving under General 
Azaersi’s leadership. The few hobgoblins who continue 
to live in Isger do so in the caverns of the Chitterwood, 
patiently biding their time until circumstances are right 
for them to make their presence known. Local goblin 
tribes rarely cooperate willingly with hobgoblins 
anymore; some, however, remain in thrall to these 
powerful hobgoblins.
NON-GOBLINOIDS
Most humans and others who aren’t of goblinoid 
ancestry choose not to live in the Chitterwood—
which is precisely why some do decide to reside 
here. Whether they make their living by preying 
upon caravans along the Chitterwood’s trade route 
or simply need a place to lie low for a while, non-
goblinoid residents appreciate the seclusion offered 
by these woods.
The town of Stumpfield is the most well-known 
of any humanoid settlements near the woods, along 
with its neighbor Fernsby. Stumpfield is unique for 
its large mix of both goblinoid and non-goblinoid 
residents. More information on Stumpfield is on 
pages 30 and 39.
MONSTERS
While goblinoids are the most well-known of the 
Chitterwood’s residents, other creatures also lurk 
in the decrepit woods. Ghosts and haunts are quite 
common, for much blood was shed during the war, 
as are polluted fey spirits twisted by the burning of 
the woods and the blood soaked into the ground. 
The most infamous of these haunts is the rumored 
goblinblood beast, a creature said to be made up 
purely of the blood shed during the war, that longs 
for violence and battle. It’s said to cause visions of 
war and fire in its victims, who believe they’re burning 
in the razing of the Chitterwood.
Dragons are also said to reside in the woods, 
though few have been seen since the Goblinblood 
Wars. Rumor has it a forest dragon is attempting

to lay claim to a large section of the Chitterwood 
and battling goblins to do so. There’s also said to 
be an ancient beast of living shadow haunting the 
Chitterwood, though no one living has been able to 
confirm its existence.
Locations
The Chitterwood houses several unique environments. 
Though much was destroyed, some survived the fires 
of the Goblinblood Wars, while others came to be 
afterward.
BARKING CAVERNS
The Spine Threshers live in the Barking Caverns, 
named for the barks of their mounts. This cave system 
is one of the most expansive in the Chitterwood, with 
wide caves that create plenty of room to run and 
train their mounts. The smaller tunnels are used for 
racing and practice, for squeezing through narrow 
passageways can prove one’s worth as a rider.
THE BIG FIRE
This large bonfire deep in the woods is said to burn 
eternally, fed and cared for by the Cinder Seekers. 
The Cinder Seekers view the Big Fire as near-sacred, 
lighting their torches from it in hopes of an extra 
powerful flame. Yet in truth, it’s an ordinary fire that 
simply hasn’t gone out thanks to the diligence of its 
keepers, who insist it’s special in every way and feed 
it only the best of kindling (including, occasionally, an 
unfortunate Isgeri Slayer). The Big Fire is protected 
from rain by a canvas tied to the tree branches 
above it, which makes its smoke billow out low to 
the ground, causing coughing fits whenever anyone 
approaches.
BURNT ENDS
The Burnt Ends is what the goblins call the edges 
of the Chitterwood where the Bulbhead goblins 
make their homes. The trees are much younger here, 
renewing after the effects of the war, and there’s less 
cover than most goblins would like. Nevertheless, the 
Bulbhead goblins call it home and have made a good 
living farming in the once-charred soil, planting their 
iconic gourds and various vegetables to trade.
FROG BOG
Frog Bog is the colloquial name for the swampy 
eastern Chitterwood, where the Mudrub goblins make 
their home. It’s a consistently soggy environment in 
the warm months, drying out in the winter. Frog Bog 
is most known for its large population of frogs as well 
as housing the frog-like Mudrub goblins.
Each year, the frogs get larger and larger, a sign that 
the Chitterwood is healing. Rumors have it that an 
enormous frog the size of a cart lives deep within the 
dirt, and many a Mudrub goblin has attempted to find 
it to lay claim to a most glorious and filling meal.
GOLDENMOUTH
Goldenmouth is the rumored hoard of the dragon 
Jurinex, said to be lost deep in the Chitterwood when 
humans burned down the landmarks that marked its 
location. Many still delve into the Chitterwood in 
attempts to find this lost treasure, braving the dangers 
of the woods in hopes of securing a valuable prize. The 
hoard is said to be a century’s worth of accumulated 
gold and treasures, along with powerful artifacts that 
can grant wishes and immortality.
SHRIEKING CAVERNS
The People of the Swarm reside in the Shrieking 
Caverns, named for the cry of the thousands of bats 
swarming in the caves. These caves are filled with 
threats like cave bears but also nourishment, such as 
fish and lichen, thanks to an underground river.
High ceilings and low pits establish a dangerous 
environment in the caverns, yet it’s also filled with 
nooks and crannies that make for the perfect resting 
spots for goblins. The humidity in the caverns makes 
lighting fires difficult at times, so goblins sometimes 
rely on glowing worms and fungi for a source of light.
STAGFALL CAVES
This set of caves has existed since ancient days, serving 
as a home and shelter to many creatures. Deep within 
the caverns is a nexus of primal power, which has 
lain dormant for centuries until the events of this 
campaign. More about the Stagfall Caves can be found 
on page 57.
SUNLESS TUNNELS
The Sunless Tunnels are where the Hookback goblins 
live in the southern Chitterwood, deep below the 
surface. These caves are uniquely rife with ores the 
goblins use to create their iconic piercings, smelting 
them with specialized techniques. Despite their limited 
use of fire, the Hookback goblins have mastered its 
use, and their tunnels are filled with valuable chunks 
of metal that would make Elidir’s wealthiest nobles 
swoon.
Something else lives deep in the tunnels, where no 
Hookback goblin dares tread. It’s unknown what 
beast breathes so heavily in the dark, but all Hookback 
goblins know not to brave the specific tunnels it can 
be heard in.

While much of Isger suffers the deprivations of war and 
four millennia’s worth of neglect from disinterested 
rulers, Elidir has few such worries. The country’s 
capital is the pumping heart at the center of the trade 
industry that is the nation’s lifeblood. Located on the 
Conerica River, the vibrant city bustles with the traffic 
of merchants coming and going between Cheliax and 
Druma, Molthune, and Andoran. They, and the guards 
and craftspeople who facilitate their industry, pour 
gold and resources into the city almost as quickly as 
Isger’s troubles can drain them again.
Despite the riches that pass through Elidir, life 
isn’t easy. Thousands of years of subservience to its 
patron states and the stripping of most of the country’s 
resources have left deep mental scars on the population. 
Such strains were exacerbated by the Goblinblood 
Wars, which devastated the countryside. Though the 
city itself saw little fighting, it has only barely recovered 
from the lost generation who marched off to battle 
and never returned, not to mention the need to care 
for thousands of orphans, refugees, and traumatized 
returning soldiers.
Such tensions play out in the behaviors of the 
city’s elite class of nobles and merchants, who take 
advantage of their position and exert what power they 
have in extravagant displays of wealth. Beneath them, 
many residents still labor in a poverty barely above the 
subsistence struggles of those in the hinterlands. Eking 
out a day-to-day existence, they struggle to rebuild 
the generational wealth lost in the Goblinblood 
Wars. Now, with the conflict of Cheliax and Andoran 
erupting in Breachill, the elites of Elidir fear that the 
unblemished capital might finally be touched by the 
nation’s troubles.
ELIDIR

their disdain for the orphans, refugees, and war veterans

to level 8 are available in the city. Uncommon items up 
to level 6 are frequently available, as is the occasional 
rare item.

which claims first choice on its resources, and its grip 
is tightest on the capital, resulting in higher prices.

History
Long before Elidir became a city under Taldan rule, 
it was a gathering place of native Isgeri tribes thanks 
to its advantageous position on the Conerica River. 
In the first millennium ar, local tribes began building 
permanent structures in the area, roundhouses used 
during the seasonal gathering of tribes to trade and 
share news.
The natural advantages the site offered were 
immediately apparent to the leaders of Taldor’s 
Seventh Army of Exploration, which made the location 
its headquarters during its campaign of pacification. 
Following the tribes’ defeat, the army’s commander 
General Xerlidia Elidos turned the sprawling camp 
into a permanent settlement, naming it after herself. It 
grew steadily for the next 2,000 years into a booming 
metropolis of 20,000 souls, becoming a center of trade 
that welcomed riches and new settlers to the town in 
equal measure.
Elidir

===== Page 191 =====
190
But the Even-Tongued Conquest proved devastating 
for the city, which became a center of the struggle 
for Isger until Cheliax firmly wrested control of the 
province from Taldor. The resources that would’ve 
let the city rebuild instead immediately 
began flowing to Isger’s new patron.
With no homes to return to, many 
of the survivors of the climactic Battle 
of Elidir departed—leaving for the 
outskirts of Isger or, if they had the 
means, to Cheliax, Taldor, and any other 
country that would take them in. With 
peace restored, Elidir was reestablished 
as a trade center but, lacking the 
resources it had in its first millennia, never 
reached its former glory again.
The country’s most recent conflict, the 
Goblinblood Wars, had little impact on the city 
itself since the elites ignored the plight 
of the countryside to protect themselves. 
The Isgeri Army was devastated by 
loss, leading Hedvend VI to order the 
remaining soldiers to protect the capital over the 
countryside. The aftereffects of this callousness have 
made a mark, as the nation is inundated with those 
who suffered because of the elites’ selfishness, and they 
resentfully remember the leaders who failed them.
Geography
The Conerica River, which first brought the Isgeri 
tribes and then Taldan settlers to Elidir, has fueled the 
city’s growth and determined its direction. Growing 
first on one bank, Elidir quickly spread to both sides 
of the Conerica, doubling the space available for ships 
to dock. In the millennia since, the city has largely 
extended up and down the length of the waterway 
instead of outward in a constant effort to increase the 
room for trade.
Because the river became the center of industry, 
Elidir’s elite built their lavish homes on the hills on the 
city’s outskirts, while the working class neighborhoods 
arose between them, insulating the elite from the noise 
and crowds of the docks and sparing them from the 
occasional floods. In a style that continues today, the 
elite’s manors often included their own walls around 
the grounds, initially to protect from bandits before 
the city built its primary wall and later to keep the 
rabble separate (especially in the event of unrest).
Located in the foothills of the Menador Mountains, 
Elidir is occasionally subjected to brutal winter storms 
that sweep off the range and dump a foot of snow 
or more on the city. Because the Conerica itself never 
stops flowing, neither does trade in the city, and such 
storms make it all the more dangerous for the laborers 
who have to deal with the snow and cold. Spring melt 
sometimes floods the Conerica, leaving Elidir a muddy 
mess that only affects the lower class due to location.
Government
Elidir is governed by the steward of 
Isger, who oversees its bureaucracy 
at the sufferance of Cheliax’s Queen 
Abrogail 
Thrune 
II. 
Because 
the 
diabolic empire cares little about what 
happens to the city as long as trade isn’t 
disrupted, the steward has a loose leash 
when it comes to the capital. To ensure 
that affairs of state continue, Hedvend 
VI has largely empowered two main forces 
in his government: the Isgeri Army and the 
Trade Office, both of which operate in close 
collaboration. The former patrols the 
Conerica Straits, keeping it safe from 
bandits and monsters, while the latter 
oversees all trade in the city, including 
managing the docks and warehouses, collecting taxes, 
tariffs, and other fees, and ensuring the labor supply 
is reliable.
Elidir’s most important laws revolve around its 
trade—for example, ships making the journey between 
Druma and Cheliax have priority over local river traffic 
(many of the city’s elite keep a ship ostensibly from 
one of those two nations to let them take advantage 
of the law). Similarly, interfering with the river trade 
brings harsh consequences. Crimes committed within 
100 yards of the river face harsher punishments than 
the same crime committed elsewhere in the city. Both 
boarding a boat without permission or sinking a boat 
are serious crimes, though they might be mitigated very 
slightly if the boat isn’t currently laden with goods.
The legacy of the Goblinblood Wars also remains in 
the city’s War Laws, supposedly temporary measures 
intended to ensure the city’s safety in the face of 
goblin threats. Dogs must be allowed to roam freely 
in the city, in the expectation that they would both 
warn of an attack and scare away goblins. Singing in 
public was also forbidden for fear it could be mistaken 
for goblin song, leading to a growing tradition of 
rebellious poetry and storytelling.
As the war ground on and deprivation deepened 
even in the city, the laws became harsher toward those 
who squandered resources. Wasting food became 
a crime punished by a lash on a first offense, up to 
imprisonment for repeated waste. Butchers were 
required to deliver the intestines of the animals they 
slaughtered to the army to be made into bowstrings.

When starvation became a concern, the law’s 
punishments against interfering with a roaming dog 
were extended and toughened for anyone who killed 
a dog. More cynically, so as to not have to waste time 
enforcing theft laws against starving masses, taking 
fruit or vegetables from someone else’s garden became 
permissible, as long as it wasn’t more than could be 
held in one hand. Enforcement of these ordinances 
today is very situational, applying far more often to 
the city’s poorer residents than to Elidir’s elite.
Residents
Following 
early 
divides 
between 
the 
Taldan 
conquerors and Isgeri tribes, the divisions between 
both cultures slowly melted away, and they become 
one, intermixing freely. Their descendants form the 
majority of the city, and it’s rare that a native Elidiran 
human can (or would even try to) define themselves as 
purely Taldan or Kellid.
Halflings form the next largest population in 
the city, thanks in large part to Isger’s vassalage to 
Cheliax. Those whose families weren’t brought to 
Elidir against their will often saw the city as a place 
where they were more likely to be able to escape 
servitude than in the heart of their diabolic homeland. 
The Emancipation Edict drew yet more halflings to 
the city, where the meager resources were offset 
by the lighter yoke of tyranny than in Cheliax.
More recently, following the founding of 
Oprak and a general cultural trend toward 
better understanding for goblins, strict rules 
forbidding goblinoids from entering Elidir have 
been forgotten. Now, many are seen as sources 
of cheap labor. Still, tensions exist between the 
human survivors of the Goblinblood Wars and 
the new goblin arrivals in the city, who carry little 
memory of their ancestors’ war.
The city’s prominent position on a major trade 
route brings plenty of traffic among other ancestries, 
some of whom choose to make their home in the city. 
While the presence of elves, dwarves, gnomes, aiuvarin, 
and dromaar as well as other ancestries and heritages 
aren’t common in Elidir, they’re certainly not unusual 
enough to draw any comment or double glances.
NOTABLE FIGURES
There are many caravanserai operators on the 
outskirts of Elidir, but few are as ambitious as Adasely 
Tisandera (opportunistic female human merchant 3). 
Having grown up poor in the lower levels of Elidir, 
Adasely longs to take control of all caravanserai 
under her name and dominate the market, flooding 
her hands with gold. She’s been working on setting 
up a caravanserai’s guild and hopes to ally with other 
merchants with similar aspirations, though she makes 
sure that none are as ambitious as herself.
Cygnetus Frawn (flamboyant nonbinary human 
dandy 9) is the foremost trendsetter in Elidir, leading 
society in both fashion and social movements. They are 
a strong supporter of Cheliax and use their seemingly 
flighty parties and fashion choices to subtly maneuver 
others into supporting the patron nation. Calling for 
charity balls, hosting masquerades, and donating to 
the church of Asmodeus all work to serve a greater 
purpose: keeping Isger in check.
Archbanker Dwingini Berylbelt (nonchalant female 
dwarf cleric of Abadar 8) is the high priest of Abadar 
in Elidir, tending to his worshippers among the city. 
She feels that Isger’s sole focus on Elidir stifles the 
spread of the market in the countryside, strangling the 
ability for more wealth and prosperity in the nation. 
She keeps quiet, however, knowing that opening her 
mouth wouldn’t serve her well.
Elidir Local

===== Page 193 =====
192
Hedvend VI (sniveling male human aristocrat 9) 
has served as Isger’s steward for decades, and his sole 
priority is to keep Cheliax content. This approach has 
led to a large wealth disparity between those in the 
capital and those outside of it, as his focus is on the 
trade around the Conerica River at the cost of ignoring 
the issues of the countryside. He’s vastly unpopular 
with the people, with even his fellow elites hoping to 
knock him down a peg and take his place.
Few are even aware of the existence of Urgathoa’s 
followers in Isger, let alone that they’re led by the 
cheerful chef Luminia Bell (zealous female human 
cleric 6). Luminia uses her day job as a fine dining 
chef to gain access to the rarest of delicacies and the 
wealthiest of patrons, bringing goods back to indulge 
in with fellow worshippers of the Pallid Princess in 
lavish feasts and debauchery. She’s very popular with 
the elites for her elaborate meals and unique food 
decorations, utilizing unusual ingredients to create the 
most indulgent meals possible in the name of gluttony.
The current scourge of merchant ships traveling 
down the Conerica River is the Queen of Conerica 
(avaricious female halfling bandit 6), a pirate captain 
who leads raids solely on trade ships. The pirates have 
learned to work extremely efficiently, finishing their 
raids within an hour and absconding with their goods 
before the authorities can catch up. Despite the large 
bounty on her head, the mysterious leader of these 
pirates is yet to be identified or arrested.
A small holy war is being waged in the streets of 
Elidir, and one side is led by Sevizoy (determined 
male dromaar human former assassin 8), the leader of 
the reformed temple of Nocticula. Sevizoy is a cleric 
with little training outside of his immense faith, a 
former assassin who changed his ways and fervently 
believes that everyone should have a chance to do the 
same. However, his opposition in the traditionalist 
worshippers of Nocticula’s demonic incarnation hunt 
down his clergy and followers, forcing him to lead 
the fight against them. Sevizoy proclaims these other 
worshippers of Nocticula heretics yet hopes they’ll 
find redemption as the Redeemer Queen did.

Elidiran society is largely shaped by its traumas—
Cheliax’s domination of the country and the 
Goblinblood Wars—and its population’s perseverance 
in the face of such tragedies. On its surface, the culture

are celebrated perfunctorily by most of the city’s 
population. Beneath that veneer, however, lies a deep 
well of both resilience and resentment.
The little-spoken truth of their subservience 
preys on the minds of Elidir’s elite, eating away at 
their confidence. With little ability to exert any 
real authority over their country, they instead fall 
back on what they can control—their own wealth. 
Many flaunt their status, living in gated manors in 
the city, where they hold grand galas and feast on 
foods imported from far-off countries. Their lavish 
lifestyles often incorporate trends and fashions seen 
in distant Egorian but remain far enough behind the 
times that visiting Chelaxians routinely make sport 
of their provincial counterparts. Such mockery only 
prods Elidir’s elites on to greater excess.
That hedonistic behavior further emphasizes the 
chasm between the city’s haves and have-nots, who 
refuse to let the deprivation they face define them. 
Many celebrate even the smallest efforts at kindness 
and helping others, pointing to their support of both 
the city’s orphans and haunted veterans after the wars 
as shining examples of Elidiran culture. Knowing 
that they might not have the ability to offer more 
to those who are struggling, Elidirans emphasize the 
importance of trying to help. In quiet voices, little 
acts of charity and kindness are known as “yanking 
the devil’s tail” to indicate the conditions imposed by 
Cheliax can’t break the Isgeri spirit.
Elidiran dress and architecture showcase the city’s 
endurance, emphasizing beauty even without the 
natural resources other capitals enjoy. Outside of the 
wealthy elite, most residents wear clothing made from 
wool, linen, or other common materials but use bright 
colors and delicate embroidery to add beauty. Glass 
beads, often sewn into shirts and dresses or worn as 
jewelry, take the place of jewels. Residents similarly 
find ways to beautify their homes without expensive 
touches, using pierced balusters, colorful glass bead 
hangings, and brightly painted frieze boards to create 
a welcoming touch.
Most Elidirans are too occupied with daily life—
whether that’s getting through the day among the 
poorest residents, or sybaritic pleasures among the 
upper classes—to devote much attention to matters of 
faith. Asmodeus, as the state religion, has the largest 
presence in the city, followed by Abadar.
There’s also a small contingent of Nocticula 
worshippers, though they’ve been split with her 
ascension to a deity, for some refuse to accept her 
as the Redeemer Queen and hunt down those who 
do. This conflict is kept to the shadows, neither side 
wanting to draw attention from the authorities.
In addition, unnoticed by the vast majority of the 
population, Urgathoa’s faith quietly lurks. Though 
the presence of Asmodeus’ church keeps them in the 
shadows, the Pallid Princess’s agents encourage the 
cultural malaise among the city’s most powerful that 
leads them into excess and, ultimately, her claws. 
They similarly seek to tempt the city’s poorer masses, 
whispering that they always deserve more, deserve 
better, in hopes that will lead them to Urgathoa. 
Their subtle machinations have led to promotions 
elsewhere for ambitious clerics of other faiths, 
ensuring the city is largely served by those who are 
less capable or interested and thus more likely to fail 
in facing Urgathoa’s growing undead army outside 
the city walls.
Relations and Conflicts
The army’s focus on protecting the Conerica Straits 
means Elidir is largely insulated from external threats. 
While bandits and undead occasionally prey on those 
traveling to or from the city, such attacks usually take 
place well out of sight of the city walls and beyond the 
reach of its armed patrols. The city’s greatest conflicts 
come from within: discontent among rich and poor 
alike, and Chelaxian rule.
The large wealth disparity within the city creates 
strong tensions between the elites and anyone not 
counted among them. To ease the tensions and keep 
the rabble down, charity events to help the less 
fortunate are held quite frequently, though they serve 
more as excuses for the wealthy to socialize than to 
help those in need.
The Battle of Hellknight Hill has aroused great 
debate about Cheliax’s rule of Isger and the rights of 
its citizens. Rebellious youths call for Hedvend to step 
down after the disaster of a foreign diplomat’s death, 
and there are even those among the elites who silently 
agree, though they have ulterior motives for wanting 
Hedvend out of the picture.
Beyond the threat of devils and Urgathoa’s 
followers, 
another 
religious 
battle 
here 
goes 
largely unnoticed by the city’s leaders. Nocticula’s 
followers—though they make up just a tiny fraction 
of the populace—wage a bloody war between those 
who have accepted her new divine role and the 
followers of her long-standing temple here devoted 
to her prior demonic incarnation. Such violence so 
far has largely been contained to Elidir’s dark alleys 
but threatens to spill out into the public.

===== Page 195 =====
194
Places of Interest
As the capital city, Elidir is the location of several 
unique and storied places. Here are some of the most 
important or interesting of those locations.
A. Caravanserai: Caravanserais nestle against the 
city’s walls, offering a place to stay for those willing to 
trade safety for ease. Guards and adventurers come to 
seek employment or companions for journeys through 
more dangerous parts of Avistan, while thieves and 
opportunists look for easy prey.
B. Chelaxian Quarter: This walled neighborhood, 
known to locals as the Devils’ Court, surrounds the 
official Thrune embassy and the wealthy homes of 
expatriates and other Chelaxians who find themselves 
in Elidir. The houses here are the most luxurious in 
all the city, and the occupants are known for their 
lifestyles of excess. Dottari and devils ensure the 
residents’ safety, brutally enforcing the law against any 
trespassers and lawbreakers.
C. Coffer Hall: The primary temple of Abadar is a 
surprisingly low-key structure considering the amount 
of wealth that flows through Elidir. That’s by design, 
as Urgathoa’s agents have long worked to ensure the 
Master of the First Vault’s most capable clerics find 
opportunities in other parts of the Inner Sea, leaving 
only those who lack grand ambition or imagination to 
cater to the city’s faithful.
D. Conerica Landing: The collection of wooden 
docks and warehouses that facilitate the city’s prime 
industry—trade—are collectively known as Conerica 
Landing. They run up and down both banks of the 
river and are some of the most heavily guarded areas 
of the city.
E. Druma Road Gate: The main overland highway 
from Druma enters Elidir at the Druma Road Gate, 
which is always crowded with caravans and others 
seeking to enter or exit. Waits to enter can reach up 
to a day here (though a little gold helps speed up the 
process) with anyone who leaves their place in line 
having to reenter at the end of the queue.
F. Elidir Academy for Proper Goblins: After the 
children raised in this former orphanage grew up and 
moved out, Ottschan Rasefel (severe nonbinary human 
caretaker 2) set their sights on a new project: educating 
goblins. Their short temper and harsh methods quickly 
drive away most young goblins who end up here, but 
the school continues to garner popular support from 
the city’s elite.
G. Grand Cheliax Gate: Two carved wooden 
statues of nessari devils tower over the wall on either 
side of this western entrance to the city, which locals 
know as the Devilsgate. Though it’s nearly as busy 
as the Druma Road Gate, it’s known for the guards’ 
efficient manner, which keeps a steady flow of traffic 
moving.
H. Gyve: The city’s prison holds debtors, political 
prisoners, and true criminals in horrid conditions. 
Subterranean torture chambers routinely extract 
confessions from the innocent and guilty alike.
I. Hedvend Park: This park is named after one of 
the earlier stewards of Isger, a stark reminder of the 
nepotism that runs rampant in Chelaxian circles. 
Hedvend VI has tried to make this park a luxurious 
experience, pouring funds to build a towering 
fountain with a likeness of Abrogail Thrune II on 
it,and importing a number of exotic birds and fish to 
decorate the landscape with.
J. The Iron Strop: This home for wounded veterans 
was run by Gorumite clerics who sought to restore 
their patients to full health—and the ability to battle 
again. Following Gorum’s death, the remaining 
caretakers and patients have become jaded nihilists, 
picking fights with anyone who passes by.
K. Home to Kazhlik: This popular, smoke-filled 
tavern has passed from one dwarven owner to another 
ever since it was founded more than 2,000 years ago. 
Though the origin of its name was forgotten until a 
recent discovery by the Pathfinder Society, it is known 
for its home-cooked meals with Five Kings Mountains 
delicacies and is a favorite of dwarves (and many 
others) who make their way through the city.
L. Isgeri Circle: Most residents give a wide berth 
to this 2,500-year-old circle of standing stones 
surrounding a badly worn altar to Urgathoa (in an 
ancient Kellid incarnation as a harvest goddess) in 
Xerlidia Park. Originally put up to help appease the 
early Isgeri, attempts to remove the circle over the 
millennia have all failed, and superstition says anyone 
who tries will grow ill and die.
M. Isger’s Fist: The Isgeri military operates out of 
this fortress complex, so-called because it wields the 
sword that is the army. Surrounding the central castle 
that hosts the command operations are barracks, 
stables, and other key elements of the country’s armed 
forces.
N. Kingsthrone Cathedral: Built with taxpayers’ 
money at the direct command of the Thrunes, this 
grand cathedral is the center of Asmodeus’ faith in 
Elidir. Its five ruby-studded towers rise high into the 
skyline, ensuring they can be seen from anywhere 
in the city. Traffic is constant at the cathedral, with 
merchants and dottari milling about outside of 
the grand doors and congregants attending strictly 
scheduled times of worship. The cathedral is the most 
popular place of worship not out of piety but fear, as 
no one wants to be seen as disloyal to Cheliax.
